en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas,
Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Fǎn Fàn.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmarakṣa and others, by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time, the World-Honored One was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, within the Dharma-realm Palace of the Wondrous Half-Moon Peak, together with a great assembly of twenty-five thousand bhikṣus. All were arhats who had exhausted all outflows and were free from all afflictions; their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated. Like great dragon kings, they had accomplished all that was to be done and completed all that was to be cultivated. Having laid down the heavy burden and attained their own benefit, they had exhausted the fetters of existence and their mental faculties were liberated. With mastery over all states of mind, they had reached the further shore. Among them, the eighteen great śrāvakas, headed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya, were the leaders of the assembly.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of seventy-two million *koṭī-nayuta* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were:

the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vasuśrī, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bodhiśrī, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, and so forth. All these bodhisattvas had skillfully turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma; they had all skillfully inquired into the vast and correct Dharma of the *Ratnakūṭa*; they dwelt on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), their wisdom being as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru; they were well able to contemplate the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-origination, and naturelessness of all phenomena, illuminating the vast, profound principles of the Dharma and the path of excellent deportment.

Furthermore, all these bodhisattvas have been dispatched from their respective worlds by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-Tathāgatas to arrive here; they are all capable of manifesting various supernormal powers and abide in the natural purity of the self-nature of all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"This assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possesses great majestic power; for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they have come from as many worlds of great majestic power as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, arriving at this assembly as swiftly as the wind."
I should now reveal and proclaim the vast, sublime Dharma, or manifest a sign of light that shines forth extensively.
Furthermore, I shall cause this assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, within this gathering, to hear the Dharma being taught and inquire about its meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a radiance that shone everywhere throughout inconceivable trichiliocosms, as numerous as the dust motes within the ten directions.

Immediately, from each of the ten directions, there arrived at this assembly bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddha-fields. Each of these bodhisattvas manifested the inconceivable supernatural powers of a bodhisattva; having arrived at the Buddha’s assembly, they each made offerings to the Buddha with inconceivable offerings of exquisite colors, and each sat upon a lotus throne produced by their own power of vows, gazing up at the World-Honored One.

At that time, within the Dharma-realm palace, there spontaneously appeared a great lion throne of the treasury of precious lotuses, equal in length and breadth to incalculable *koṭi* yojanas and rising in stages of increasing height. It was composed of various *maṇi* jewels of radiant light, with boundary paths made of *maṇi* jewels of lightning-light, lotus stalks made of *maṇi* jewels of inconceivable light, and interspersed with incomparable *maṇi* jewels. Exquisite garlands were fashioned from *maṇi* jewels of light surpassing all analogy, while nets of *maṇi* jewels of sovereign kings hung down to cover it above; various canopies, banners, and pennants of *maṇi* jewels of manifold radiance were erected.

And upon that great maṇi-jewel lotus-treasury lion throne, there universally appeared ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light, which illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, from each of the ten directions, there gathered an assembly of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protecting devas (lokapālas), equal in number to the unspeakable atoms of ten buddha-fields.
Within these, some are situated in jeweled pavilions where inconceivable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of celestial maidens play exquisite music;
some are situated in pavilions made of wonderful flowers; some in pavilions made of dragon-firm sandalwood incense;
some in pavilions made of pearls; and some in pavilions made of great diamond-jewels.
In some places, there were pavilions made of *vajra-prabhāsa-maṇi-ratna*; in some places, pavilions made of pure gold;
in some places, pavilions made of the sovereign king of *maṇi* jewels that gathers all radiance;
in some places, pavilions made of *īśvararāja-maṇi-ratna*; and in some places, pavilions made of *cintāmaṇi*.
There were pavilions made of various materials— some made of *indranīla* mani jewels,
some made of great *mahāmaṇi* jewels that were pure, adorned, and universally radiant within the midst of the great ocean—
and in all of them were incalculable, inconceivable hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of celestial maidens who played [musical instruments].
Exquisite musical instruments came through the air;
having arrived at the Buddha’s assembly, they all presented inconceivable, peerless, and measureless offerings of supreme excellence.
Having made offerings to the Buddha, each [bodhisattva] gazed upon the World-Honored One from within a seat produced by their own power of vows.

At that time, this trichiliocosm was entirely transformed into the exquisite color and appearance of Jāmbūnada gold; there spontaneously appeared various trees adorned with mani-jewels, trees of exquisite garments, and trees of dragon-firm sandalwood incense. Nets of *vidyutprabha* mani-jewels formed of wondrous gems hung down to cover them, while precious canopies, banners, and streamers were erected.

Among all those trees, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of asankhyeya celestial maidens, each holding half-body-length pearl necklaces or, alternatively, holding garlands of mani jewels.
At that time, from within that great maṇi-jewel lotus-treasury lion throne, a voice spontaneously spoke these verses:
“The King among Men has come to this seat; He is born from the power of his original merit.
May he cause all the aspirations of the multitude to be perfectly fulfilled; Supreme among bipeds, may you graciously accept him.”
This body of mine is composed of jewels; within it, one jewel is the lotus seat.
According to the inclinations of the Honored One among Men, this Savior of the World is able to fulfill all aspirations.
This present lotus seat made of jewels is the most sublime and wondrous in this world;
for the sake of millions of beings, he expounds the Dharma-gate, so that all who hear it may attain this very seat.
Your body manifests the mark of a thousand rays of light, Universally illuminating all worlds;
Beholding this mark, joy arises within me; I pray that the Buddha will now accept this seat of mine.
Having swiftly taken his seat, he has accepted me; this seat has been occupied eight koṭis of times.
Now the Muni, the Honored One of Natural Wisdom, ascends the seat and universally embraces all classes of beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his original seat and sat cross-legged upon the lion throne of the precious lotus treasury. He surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, wishing to proclaim the most supreme and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the entire assembly of great bodhisattvas all had this thought:

"It would be a source of great fortune if we were now to hear the profound, true Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing as requested by the youthful Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"

At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who was already present in the assembly, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the multitude of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has spoken of as 'non-arising' and 'non-ceasing,' of which dharma is this the designation (adhivacana)?"
He then spoke a verse to pose his inquiry:
“Non-arising and non-ceasing—this is what the Buddha has taught.
What are the characteristics of Great Wisdom, and how are they expounded herein?”
If phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, then they would be without view and without cause;
how then could the Buddha, the Great Muni, have proclaimed them?
These Bodhisattvas from the ten directions were sent here by all the Buddhas for this very reason.
“Seeking the dharma-gate of great wisdom, we pray that the Honored One will preach the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Mañjuśrī! You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding such principles.

According to your intention, you will bring great benefit to many people; out of compassion for the world, you will cause them to practice so that they may universally attain peace and happiness, and you will further be able to bring benefit and joy to all the hosts of devas and humans.

These great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have now come here do not give rise to fear for the sake of attaining the stage of Buddhahood; they act in this place without dread, nor do they experience any alarm or terror.
Mañjuśrī! All of them are encompassed by true wisdom.
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata now teaches such a Dharma, namely: non-arising and non-ceasing.
Mañjuśrī! That which is neither born nor extinguished is a designation for the Tathāgata.

It is, for example, like the appearance of the great earth formed from vaidūrya jewels; within that appearance of the great earth, there exists the vast, magnificent palace where Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
And that Lord of Devas constantly dwells therein, experiencing the five celestial sensual pleasures, supreme and wondrous bliss, and sporting with sovereign ease.
Those hosts of devas call out to all the people within this Jambudvīpa—whether men, women, boys, or girls—and say:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"You should all observe the Great, Vast, and Victorious Hall of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wherein the Lord enjoys supreme and wondrous bliss.
You should come here and extensively practice giving, cultivate meritorious deeds, and accumulate virtuous conduct."

"You should all know that this Great Palace of Universal Excellence, where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, now resides, is endowed with supernormal powers. You ought to cultivate meritorious deeds so that you may obtain a reward like that of the Lord of the Devas, dwelling peacefully in the celestial palace and enjoying supreme, wondrous bliss."

At that time, all the people in Jambudvīpa—whether men, women, boys, or girls—beheld this Great Palace of Universal Victory belonging to Śakra, Lord of Devas, composed of Vaiḍūrya jewel upon the great earth. Having seen it, they joined their palms, took up fragrant flowers, scattered them toward the sky, and spoke these words:
"May we also obtain such a state in the future, so that like Śakra, Lord of Devas, we may dwell in the Palace of Universal Victory, enjoying supreme and wondrous bliss with sovereign play."

Yet that multitude of people was entirely unaware that the lapis lazuli ground was manifesting as a reflection, nor that the Great and Vast Victorious Palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is composed of pure substance, appeared like a reflection.

Mañjuśrī! Because that Lord Śakra practiced extensive generosity, cultivated meritorious deeds, and accumulated virtuous conduct, and because the power of his past roots of goodness was fully matured, he experienced those supreme and wondrous palaces in that celestial realm.

Mañjuśrī! That ground of vaidūrya does not exist inherently; neither do the Trāyastriṃśa gods nor the Great Palace of Vast Excellence where Śakra, Lord of Devas, resides. All these are reflections produced by purity that appear before one and are ever-present, yet they truly neither arise nor cease.
“Mañjuśrī! All sentient beings are likewise; if they contemplate with a pure mind according to reality, the Tathāgata will manifest his physical form before them.
Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power, he causes all sentient beings to behold the Tathāgata.”

Yet, fundamentally, it is without reality—neither arising nor ceasing; it has no nature, yet is not without nature; it has no perception, yet is not without perception; it is neither mundane nor non-mundane; it has no form, yet is not without form.
"Mañjuśrī! All sentient beings take the reflected image of the Tathāgata as their object of focus, scattering incense, flowers, robes, and exquisite jewels as offerings, and speak these words:
'May I, in the future, obtain supreme and wondrous retribution, becoming equal to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"

Those sentient beings, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, extensively practice giving, cultivate meritorious deeds, and accumulate virtuous conduct, dedicating these merits with the vow that they shall attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! It is like the great earth formed of vaidūrya gemstone, wherein the reflection of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, appears. It is without movement or shifting, without reception, and without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is without discrimination, yet not separate from discrimination; without calculation, yet not separate from calculation. It is not a product of volitional thought or mental attention (*manasikāra*); it is tranquil and cool, unborn and unceasing. It is without seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or perceiving; it is without designation and without manifestation."

Mañjuśrī! In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: without movement or transition, without reception, and without conceptual proliferation; without discrimination, yet not apart from discrimination; without deliberation, yet not apart from deliberation; not a product of volitional mental engagement, quiescent and cool, without arising or ceasing; without seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or perceiving; without designation and without manifestation.

In this way, the Tathāgatas have no place of birth or destination; all that they manifest is like a reflection. According to the differences in the faith and understanding of sentient beings, they manifest various physical forms and limits to their lifespan, solely for the purpose of maturing the power of those beings' faith and understanding.

Those sentient beings who are vessels for bodhi will appear before them; according to their inclinations and according to their faith and understanding, they cause all sentient beings to hear the essentials of the Dharma, so that they may know the characteristics of the three vehicles as they desire, and attain liberation entirely according to their aspirations.

“Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, it is like the Lord Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, who, through the accomplishment of his power of merit, possesses a great Dharma-drum that emits the sublime sound of the Dharma. It resides in the vast, expansive, and supreme palace within the midst of space, yet even those sons of gods cannot perceive it, however much they strain their eyes to look.”

Mañjuśrī! If the multitude of devaputras in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven become addicted to dalliance and play, delighting themselves with the five desires and their minds becoming negligent, such that they take no pleasure in entering the Hall of Good Dharma to chant the sounds of the Dharma; or if at times Śakra, Lord of Devas, likewise indulges in the pleasures of the five desires and becomes negligent, failing to occupy the Dharma seat to preach the Dharma for the assembly—then that great Dharma drum, situated in the midst of space, visible from afar yet transcending the realm of the eyes so as to be invisible to sight, will spontaneously produce a sound to enlighten and awaken the devaputras, saying:
"O virtuous ones!"
Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are impermanent phenomena; at this time, you must not give way to negligence, lest you quickly lose your palaces.

All conditioned formations are suffering, all conditioned formations are empty, and all phenomena are without self; do not be negligent, for this aggregate of suffering will cease and one will be reborn in another realm.
"O virtuous ones!

You should diligently chant and recite the True Dharma; sport in the garden of Dharma, seek the reality of the Dharma, and take delight in the True Dharma. By attending to and reflecting upon the True Dharma, you shall not be separated from the enjoyments of the five desires within the heavens."

"Mañjuśrī! However, that great Dharma drum is without discrimination and free from the absence of discrimination; it transcends the realm of the eye, is neither arising nor ceasing, has emerged from the path of language, and is beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness."

The Dharma-sound produced by that great Dharma-drum constantly awakens, startles, and terrifies those celestial hosts who are deluded and confused, causing them to immediately enter the Hall of Good Dharma to chant the True Dharma. They sport in the Garden of Dharma, seek the reality of the Dharma, and take delight in the True Dharma; within the True Dharma, they attend to it with mindfulness and mental attention. Having passed away from the celestial realm, they are reborn in a superior state.
Furthermore, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, enters the Hall of Good Dharma and takes his place upon the Dharma throne, he proclaims the essentials of the Dharma to the assembly of devas.

Should the time come that the celestial hosts are defeated in battle against the asura hordes, that great Dharma drum spontaneously emits a sound; at this, the asura hosts become terrified and bewildered, fleeing in all directions.
"Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, that Dharma drum has no mark of self; it is beyond verbal expression and naturally vanishes.

This Great Dharma Drum has nothing upon which to gaze; it abides in reality. It is without mind and without thought, without marks, without form, without sound, and without intrinsic nature. Moreover, it is non-dual and transcends the sphere of the eye."

“Mañjuśrī! Because of the past virtuous karma of the assembly of devaputras in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a great Dharma-drum that produces the sublime sound of the Dharma, causing all disturbances and secondary afflictions of those celestial hosts to be completely stilled. That great Dharma-drum is ever-present, yet it is without mind and without thought; it is without marks, without form, without sound, and without intrinsic nature, and it is also non-dual.”

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he is without seeing and without observation, yet he is ever-present; he is without the mark of self, without mind, and without thought; he is without marks, without form, without sound, and without intrinsic nature, transcending the sphere of the eye. Yet, according to the karmic retribution of the past merits of sentient beings and in accordance with their faith and understanding, he utters the voice of the Dharma to enlighten them. Because they hear this voice of the Dharma, all the disturbances and secondary afflictions of sentient beings are brought to complete stillness. You should know that this voice of the Dharma is itself the voice of the Tathāgata.

Mañjuśrī! These sounds of the Dharma have no substantial reality; the Tathāgata merely establishes them through skillful means for the sake of all the world. According to the karmic retributions of the past virtues of sentient beings, the Tathāgata produces the sounds of the Dharma, so that each sentient being may attain understanding according to their respective inclinations. This is to cause all sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness, and to awaken all those who are heedless.
Mañjuśrī! Once all sentient beings have heard the sound of the Dharma, they all aspire to attain the physical marks of a Tathāgata.

Those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, as well as all foolish ordinary beings, take the birth of the Tathāgata’s wholesome dharmas as their object of focus, thereby enabling them to hear the Tathāgata’s sound of the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī! The profound principle of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—namely, that which is neither born nor extinguished—should be understood in this way.

The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas,

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Commissioned Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, during the Western Heaven Translation Era. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"

For example, when the end of the summer heat draws near and the first month of the rainy season is about to arrive, by virtue of the karmic retribution of the past deeds of all sentient beings, all seeds within this great earth—cereals, medicinal herbs, and forest trees—all grow and flourish.
At that time, in the void of space, great winds blew and struck, and great torrents of water poured down.
At that moment, the entire earth was thoroughly nourished.
All the people throughout Jambudvīpa, having seen these signs, were filled with joy; their hearts were contented and delighted as they perceived that great clouds had arisen over this world.
"Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a great mass of water flowing from the sky onto the earth. At that time, all the people in Jambudvīpa would think:
'Now that this great flood is pouring over the earth, could it not be that a great cloud has arisen within it?'"
Having formed this thought, they all spoke these words:
"How marvelous! The great clouds have poured down their rain, and the vast waters fill the great earth!"

"Mañjuśrī! That great body of water does not belong to the clouds, nor is it a manifestation of the clouds; rather, because it is struck by a great wind, there is a great expanse of water filling the earth."

That very mass of water, through the power of the retribution of the past karma of those sentient beings, gradually disappears; it is sustained by the wind and dispersed by the wind, like clouds pouring down rain.

Mañjuśrī! It is solely due to the karmic retribution of sentient beings from past lives that a great torrent of water pours down from the sky; it does not belong to the clouds, nor is it produced by the clouds. The clouds have no place of origin, nor do they enter through the mind; they are free from coming and going.

It is likewise for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose roots of goodness have matured, as well as for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings; that is to say, because they have accumulated superior practices and planted roots of goodness according to their inclinations and wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world to demonstrate the path to nirvāṇa to all sentient beings, manifesting it without obstruction. When the Tathāgata dwells among the assembly of devas and humans, whatever names he establishes in his teachings are entirely without distinction.
Mañjuśrī! You should know that the sounds uttered by the Tathāgata among the assemblies of devas and humans have no reality; they are entirely non-existent. Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata is without marks, for he is free from all marks; he has no location, yet is not separate from locations; he is not established by any reality, and is without birth or cessation. Having extensively taught the True Dharma to the world of devas and humans according to their needs and having fully satisfied them, those newly resolved bodhisattvas and ordinary ignorant beings—who were to be converted through the ripening of their past virtuous karma and their delight in the dharma of nirvāṇa—do not see the Tathāgata appearing before them, and all say that the Tathāgata has entered great parinirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī! Whether the Tathāgata arises or ceases, he is entirely non-existent, because the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is neither born nor extinguished.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is primordially quiescent; the Tathāgata has no substantial reality.

Just as with the great waters, their objective referent is unreal and the clouds are likewise unreal; being without arising and without cessation, because the clouds are unreal, they are merely provisionally designated within the world.
The objects of reference for all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are likewise thus: they lack substantial reality and are neither born nor extinguished, being primordially so.
Within this dharma of non-arising, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, provisionally establishes names for the sake of the world.

“Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, it is like the Great Brahmā King, the most supreme among the supreme, who has attained mastery over thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms—that is, one hundred times three thousand great trichiliocosms—and observes all the celestial hosts day after day, reaching as far down as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings as its limit.”

Because the Great Brahmā King constantly observes all the heavens, whenever the various hosts of devaputras each enjoy the five sensual pleasures within their respective heavens, and having finished those enjoyments, play music and sing, and then, having ceased these activities, set aside all such pleasures, they each join their palms in reverence and respect, gazing up at the Brahmā King without blinking for even a moment. These hosts of devaputras each pray and entreat that the Great Brahmā King appear in the world to bring their roots of goodness to maturity.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King appears in an instant.

When the celestial retribution of this Great Brahmā King is exhausted, another Great Brahmā King establishes his palace; within ten or a hundred trichiliocosms, he attains mastery through the power of his past vows.

Those sons of gods there also have their past roots of goodness matured, whereby they perceive that Great Brahmā King daily observing all the celestial hosts, until the Great Brahmā King appears in an instant.

Mañjuśrī! That Great Brahmā King is entirely non-existent and has no location; he is without movement or transition, being utterly empty and without reality. He is without letters, without sound, without speech, without intrinsic nature, without thought, and without marks. He is beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness, and is without arising or ceasing. Yet, he manifests in accordance with the needs of the assembly of those devaputras, because of the power of the vows and roots of goodness established by the Great Brahmā King in past lives, and because the roots of goodness of the assembly of devaputras have also matured.
Yet those hosts of devaputras do not form such a thought:

"Now this Great Brahmā Heaven King manifests all manner of emanations with mastery over space; they are without reality and without letters, without sound and without speech, without intrinsic nature and without characteristics, beyond thought and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, neither arising nor ceasing."

“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: he is sovereign over emptiness, without reality, without letters, without sound, and without speech; without intrinsic nature, without characteristics, beyond thought, free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and without arising or ceasing.”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is established solely through the power of the vows and practices of a bodhisattva in former times;

furthermore, he is established through the maturation of the roots of virtue from former times of those newly resolved bodhisattvas, as well as all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and foolish ordinary beings. As it is said:

Having appeared in the world adorned with hundreds of thousands of marks, all are like reflections—devoid of location, devoid of movement, and without any bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds;
there are no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, foolish ordinary beings, nor is there any Tathāgata exercising mastery over emptiness. There is nothing at all.
Reality is without words, without sounds, and without speech; it is without intrinsic nature and without characteristics;
it is beyond thought and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is without birth and without cessation.

Mañjuśrī! Because all phenomena are empty, the physical marks of the Tathāgata are adorned with hundreds of thousands of varieties of signs; he manifests the various modes of conduct of a Tathāgata and establishes the applications of all dharmas, expounding the vast Dharma according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings. The teachings he proclaims cause all the disturbances and secondary afflictions of sentient beings to be completely stilled.
The Tathāgata is impartial; he abides in equanimity toward all things, free from all doubt and without distinction.
Mañjuśrī! For this reason, you should know that "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" are both merely metaphorical designations for the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata is the eternally unborn nature of all phenomena; All dharmas are equal to the Sugata.
To grasp at signs is folly; No real dharma revolves within the world.”
The Tathāgata’s realization is like a reflection; all wholesome dharmas are entirely without outflows.
All things pervade the Buddha’s true suchness, appearing in the world as three kinds of reflections.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Just as the light of the sun travels across Jambudvīpa, rising from the east, first illuminating Sumeru, the King of Mountains; next, illuminating the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains; next, illuminating all other great mountains; next, illuminating the Black Mountains; next, illuminating all high and prominent regions; and finally, illuminating all the low-lying regions of this Jambudvīpa—yet that sunlight is entirely without discrimination and does not depart from non-discrimination; it is neither thought nor non-thought, being free from mind, intellect, and consciousness."

Furthermore, the radiance of the sun is without arising and without ceasing, and it is devoid of all characteristics; because it is free from characteristics, it is further without volitional mental engagement (*manasikāra*); because it is free from volitional mental engagement, it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because it is free from conceptual proliferation, it is free from all affliction and harm. Because it is free from affliction and harm, it is neither this nor that, neither high nor low, neither bound nor liberated, neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom, neither possessing afflictions nor being free from afflictions, neither true speech nor false speech, neither this shore nor the other shore, neither level nor uneven, neither water nor land, neither with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) nor free from applied and sustained thought, and neither form (*rūpa*) nor non-form.
"Mañjuśrī! Just as because the great earth has high, low, and middle elevations, the illumination of light also manifests the distinctions of lower, middle, and upper reflections;
so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is neither born nor extinguished."
It is devoid of all marks and characteristics; because it is free from marks, there is no mental engagement (*manasikāra*);
because it is free from mental engagement, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because it is free from conceptual proliferation, there is no affliction or harm.
Because it is free from affliction and harm, it is neither this nor that, neither high nor low, neither bound nor liberated, and neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom.
Neither possessing afflictions nor free from afflictions; neither true speech nor false speech; neither this shore nor the other shore;
neither level nor uneven; neither water nor land; neither omniscience nor non-omniscience;
neither discursive thought and investigation nor free from discursive thought and investigation; neither accumulation nor non-accumulation.
It is neither accumulation nor non-accumulation; neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness;
neither thought nor freedom from thought; neither mind-born nor not mind-born; neither name nor non-name; neither form nor non-form;
neither speech nor non-speech; neither manifestation nor non-manifestation; neither seeing nor non-seeing; and it is not the objective domain of the eye.
It is not the non-object of the eye; it is neither that which opens the way nor that which does not open the way; it is neither the attainment of fruit nor the non-attainment of fruit;
it is neither discrimination nor non-discrimination; it is neither the departure from discrimination nor the non-departure from discrimination.
“Mañjuśrī! The sun-disk radiance of the Tathāgata shines universally throughout the triple world; that which it illuminates is likewise without obstruction of center or periphery.”

The light of the sun of wisdom emitted by the Tathāgata first illuminates the great, deep, and solid mountains that are the bodhisattvas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings who abide in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings who abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; next, it illuminates those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are firm and deep and who possess faith and understanding; and finally, it illuminates those who cling to extreme views and those sentient beings of the group fixed in error.

The light of the sun of wisdom emitted by the Tathāgata is solely for the purpose of maturing and nurturing all sentient beings, for producing the causes of the future, and for increasing the speech of wholesome dharmas.
The Tathāgata is impartial; he abides in equanimity toward all things, free from all doubt and without distinction.
Mañjuśrī! The radiant light of the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom does not form such thoughts:
"These classes of sentient beings possess great faith and understanding; I shall preach the vast Dharma for them.
These classes of sentient beings do not require the preaching of the Dharma, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination."

These types of sentient beings possess the faith and understanding of bodhisattvas; these types of sentient beings possess the faith and understanding of pratyekabuddhas; these types of sentient beings possess the faith and understanding of śrāvakas; these types of sentient beings have noble aspirations; and these types of sentient beings have inferior and perverse intentions.
Furthermore, one does not entertain such thoughts as:
"To this being of great faith and understanding, I shall preach the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;
to this being of middling faith and understanding, I shall preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas."
To those sentient beings below who possess faith and understanding, I shall preach the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.
To those sentient beings who possess such noble aspirations and right view, I shall purify their intentions.
"Even for those sentient beings who abide in the category of the fixed in error, I shall preach the Dharma according to their inclinations.
Yet the light of the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom does not give rise to such various discriminations.
Why is this? The radiant light of the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom illuminates and shatters all conceptualization, pervasive imagination, and that which arises from such conceptualization. Mañjuśrī!

"You should know that because there are differences in the various inclinations of sentient beings, the illumination of the sun-like light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise differentiated. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"

Furthermore, it is like a great maṇi jewel within the vast ocean that can fulfill all aspirations; when placed atop a high banner, it spontaneously produces sounds according to the various inclinations of sentient beings, causing them to become aware and enabling them to obtain whatever they desire.

Yet that great maṇi jewel is entirely without discrimination, yet not apart from discrimination; it is neither mind nor apart from mind; it is neither thought nor non-thought; it is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is also like this: he is without discrimination yet not apart from discrimination; he is neither mind nor apart from mind; he is neither thought nor without thought; he is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*). He has no grasper and nothing to be grasped; there is nothing to be attained and nothing already attained; there is no truth of differentiation. He is without greed, without hatred, and without delusion; he is without reality and without unreality; he is neither permanent nor impermanent; he is without radiance and not without radiance; he is neither worldly nor non-worldly. He is without applied thought (*vitarka*) and without sustained thought (*vicāra*); he is without arising and without cessation; he is neither thought nor apart from thought. He has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is empty of intrinsic nature; he has no exiting and no entering; there is no nature to be grasped, for he is beyond verbal expression, as all verbal expression has been severed.
There is no delight and no aversion, because delight has been severed;
there is no measure, because it is free from measure;
there is no realm of rebirth nor any destination toward which one proceeds, because all realms of existence have been cut off.

Because all modes of activity have been completely severed, there is no seeing, no contemplating, and nothing to be grasped; it is neither receptive nor non-receptive, neither conjoined nor disjoined, without discrimination, without conceptualization, without obstruction, and without indication. It is neither defiled nor pure; it has no name and no form-characteristics; it has no karma and no karmic retribution; it has no past, no future, and no present; not even the slightest dharma can be obtained. It is without letters and without sound, for it is free from all sounds; it is without marks, for it is free from all marks; it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between, yet there is nothing therein that can be apprehended.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata’s jewel-like wisdom is profoundly pure in its deep resolve; he plants the supreme and victorious banner of great compassion and, according to the inclinations, aspirations, and understandings of sentient beings, utters sublime sounds and teaches the Dharma as appropriate, causing all sentient beings to fully comprehend it.
The Tathāgata is impartial; he abides in equanimity toward all things, free from all doubt and without distinction. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Like an echo responding to a sound, sentient beings perceive that echoing sound; yet this sound has no reality. It is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present. It is neither internal nor external, nor is it found in between. It is without arising and without cessation; it is neither annihilated nor eternal. It is neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom; neither possessing insight (*prajñā*) nor lacking insight. It is neither clarity nor non-clarity; neither liberation nor non-liberation. It is neither with fault nor without fault; neither with mindfulness nor without mindfulness. It is neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither sitting nor not sitting. It is not the earth element, nor the water, fire, or wind elements. It is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); neither conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor free from conceptual proliferation. It is neither with volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*) nor without volitional construction; neither seeing nor non-seeing.
It is without letters and without sound, for it transcends all sounds;
it is not subject to measurement, for it exceeds all measurement;
it is without characteristics, for it is free from all marks.

It is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil; neither long nor short; neither thought nor non-thought; neither with form nor without form; neither mundane nor non-mundane. The intrinsic nature of all views is empty; it is without recollection, without mental application, without vitarka, and without vicāra. It is free from mind, mentation, and consciousness; it is equal in all places, transcends all conceptualization, and lies beyond the three periods of time.

“Mañjuśrī! The various sounds produced by the Tathāgata are all like echoes; they arise solely in accordance with the diverse inclinations of all sentient beings, being manifested as appropriate sounds so that all sentient beings may attain understanding.”

The Tathāgata is likewise: he is not of the past, future, or present; he is neither internal nor external, nor is he found in between. He is neither born nor extinguished, neither interrupted nor eternal. He is neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom, neither possessing insight nor lacking insight, neither luminous nor non-luminous, neither liberated nor unliberated, neither guilty nor guiltless, neither mindful nor unmindful, neither abiding nor non-abiding, neither sitting nor not sitting. He is not the earth element, nor the water, fire, or wind elements. He is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor free from conceptual proliferation, neither seeing nor non-seeing.
It is without letters and without sound, for it transcends all sound;
it is not subject to measurement, for it exceeds all measurement;
it is without characteristics, for it is free from all marks.

It is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil; neither long nor short; neither volitional thought nor non-volitional thought; neither having form nor being formless; neither worldly nor non-worldly. The intrinsic nature of all views is empty; it is without recollection, without mental application, without vitarka, and without vicāra. It is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is equal in all places, transcending all conceptualization, and surpassing the three periods of time.

“Mañjuśrī! In accordance with the various inclinations and diverse dispositions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata emits sublime sounds and teaches the Dharma as is appropriate, causing all sentient beings to fully understand it.”

For example, just as in the world all forests and medicinal herbs depend upon the earth and are established by it, whereby they are all able to grow and increase extensively; yet that great earth has no discrimination and is not apart from non-discrimination—it is equal in all places, without discriminatory distinctions, and free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.

All sentient beings are likewise thus: they rely upon the Tathāgata, for it is by the Tathāgata’s establishment that all roots of goodness are brought to birth and grow extensively and abundantly. This includes those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle, as well as other outsiders, brahmins, Nirgranthas, and so forth—in short, all those of heterodox views, even down to sentient beings of the fixed category of the wrong (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi). Whatever roots of goodness each of them possesses, they all rely upon the Tathāgata’s establishment, whereby they are all brought to birth and grow extensively and abundantly.

Nevertheless, the Buddha-Tathāgata is entirely without conceptual discrimination, yet is not separate from it, because all conceptual discriminations—the objects of focus for such discrimination and all mental engagements—have been completely severed. "Mañjuśrī!..."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; he is without vitarka or vicāra, without observation or demonstration, without reflection or mental engagement, abiding in equanimity toward all things without any distinction.

For example, like space, it is in all places without high or low, and without differentiation; it is without arising or ceasing, and is not of the past, future, or present. It has no form or characteristics and is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is without representation, without attachment, without measure, and without analogy. It is without establishment and without anything to be grasped; it transcends the sphere of the eye and is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness, even surpassing the path of all speech, abiding nowhere at all in any place.
