Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
Because the characteristics and states of sentient beings are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior, one might say that space itself has inferior, middling, and superior qualities.
It is likewise with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
he is equal in all places, without differentiation or discrimination, neither arising nor ceasing, and is not of the past, future, or present.
It is without form or characteristics, without conceptual proliferation; it is without indication, without designation; it is without tactile sensation, without attachment;
it is beyond all measurement, transcending all measures; it is without analogy, surpassing all analogies; it is without abiding, without grasping;
it transcends the domain of the eye and is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is without appearance.
It is without words, without sounds, and without mental activity; it has no emergence and no entry, no high and no low, transcending the realm of speech.

It accords with knowledge and enters into all places, yet because sentient beings possess inferior, middling, and superior natures, they perceive the Tathāgata as having inferior, middling, and superior aspects.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not form such a thought as:
"Now, for this class of sentient beings with inferior faith and understanding, I shall manifest an inferior physical form."
For this class of sentient beings with middling faith and understanding, I shall manifest a body of middling appearance;
for this class of sentient beings with superior faith and understanding, I shall manifest a body of superior appearance.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is also like this: he speaks to sentient beings with but a single voice, yet each according to their kind attains understanding.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not form such thoughts as:
"This class of sentient beings has inferior faith and understanding; I shall preach the Śrāvaka vehicle for them."
For those sentient beings with middling faith and understanding, I shall preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
for those sentient beings with superior faith and understanding, I shall preach the Dharma of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not form such thoughts:
"These types of sentient beings have faith and understanding in giving; I shall preach the Dharma of the perfection of giving for them.

These types of sentient beings have faith and understanding in ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; I shall preach the Dharmas of those various perfections for them."
The Tathāgata does not give rise to discrimination among all phenomena.

Why is this? Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is ultimately unborn; since the Tathāgata is unborn, he does not proclaim through name-and-form nor follow the turning of consciousness. In a single kṣaṇa, the Tathāgata is momentarily without discrimination. Because the Tathāgata possesses inexhaustible marks, and because both the limit of exhaustion and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) are definitively established, this is the state of equality of all phenomena.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is equal in all respects, without the conceptual differentiation of inferior, middling, or superior;
likewise, all phenomena are equal, without the conceptual differentiation of inferior, middling, or superior.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are unattainable. "Mañjuśrī!..."

If all phenomena are unattainable, then all phenomena are equal; if phenomena are equal, then phenomena are eternally abiding; if they are eternally abiding, they are unmoving; if they are unmoving, they are without dependence. If all phenomena have no basis of reliance, then the mind has no place to dwell; because the mind dwells nowhere, it is unborn yet arises.

If one contemplates in this manner, then the mind and mental factors proceed without inversion. That non-inverted mind is attained exactly as described; if it is attained as described, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If there is no conceptual proliferation, there is no activity. If there is no activity, there is no dispersion. If there is no dispersion, there is no accumulation. If phenomena are without dispersion, then the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not contradicted. If the nature of phenomena is not contradicted, then one accords with all things. If one accords with all things, then the self-nature of phenomena is unmoving. If the self-nature of phenomena is unmoving, then the self-nature of phenomena is what is realized. If the self-nature of phenomena is that which is realized, then there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be analytically determined.
Why is this? One should know that it is because they have a nature produced by causes and conditions.

That which has a nature produced by causes and conditions is ultimately unarisen; that which is ultimately unarisen attains tranquility; that which attains tranquility means that all mental engagements with phenomena (*dharmamanasikāra*) are equally without support. When all mental engagements with phenomena are equally without support, there is no basis whatsoever. When there is no basis, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment. When there is neither attainment nor non-attainment, one attains the permanence of phenomena. When one attains the permanence of phenomena, one accords with the profound and solid Dharma. When one accords with the profound and solid Dharma, there is not even the slightest phenomenon upon which to dwell, nor is there any "Buddha-dharma."
Why is this? Because it is the thorough realization of the nature of emptiness.
If one thoroughly realizes the nature of emptiness, that itself is bodhi.
Thus, because one fully awakens to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-activity, non-attachment, non-arising, non-grasping, and non-reliance, this itself is bodhi.

Awakening (bodhi) is associated with the profound and solid Dharma; it is by virtue of this that the designation "association" is established. Therefore, it is the association of the Dharma that is neither high nor low; the association of non-action and non-non-action; the association of neither bondage nor liberation; the association of neither a single nature nor manifold natures; and the association of neither coming nor going—this is precisely the association with the profound and solid Dharma.
If one is in accord with the profound and firm Dharma, there is nothing with which to be in accord, nothing to be abandoned, and furthermore, no fruit to be realized. Why is this?
Because the fundamental nature of the mind-dharmas is inherently luminous; it is merely defiled by adventitious afflictions, yet these cannot truly stain its essential nature.
If the intrinsic nature is luminous, there are no afflictions; if there are no afflictions, there is no antidote, because all afflictions are completely severed by means of an antidote.
Why is this so? There is no purity already attained and no purity yet to be attained; it is not apart from purity, for it has been thus from the very beginning.
That which is pure is unborn; that which is unborn is unmoving; that which is unmoving severs all forms of delight, and all that is cherished is likewise severed and extinguished.
If all cravings cease, there is no further arising; if dharmas do not arise, that is bodhi; if it is bodhi, it is equality; if it is equality, it is suchness.

If suchness is all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena and yet abides in none of them, and if within suchness there are no such conditioned or unconditioned phenomena—that is, the non-dual designation—then that which is the non-dual designation of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is itself suchness.
If that suchness is non-different suchness, if non-different suchness is non-classified suchness,
if non-classified suchness is non-coming suchness, if non-coming suchness is non-going suchness,
if non-going suchness is suchness as it has been described, if as it has been...
To speak of suchness is to speak of the suchness of non-arising; if it is the suchness of non-arising, then there is neither defilement nor purity.
If there is neither defilement nor purity, then there is neither arising nor ceasing.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then there is the equality of nirvāṇa. If there is the equality of nirvāṇa, then there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
If there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa, then there is no past, future, or present;
if there is no past, future, or present, then there are no inferior, middling, or superior dharmas;
if there are no inferior, middling, or superior dharmas, that is itself suchness (tathatā). The name "suchness" arises from...
This is the establishment.
Here, *tathatā* (suchness) is also called *bhūtadharmatā* (the nature of reality); here, *bhūtadharmatā* is also called *tathatā*; and what is called *tathatā* is precisely *tathatā*.
Suchness and the self are fundamentally non-dual and without distinction; this meaning of non-duality is itself bodhi. Bodhi has the meaning of "awakened realization.

This explained meaning is precisely the wisdom that enters the three gates of liberation, the wisdom that proclaims all phenomena, and the understanding and entry into the equality of the three periods of time for all phenomena—the sense in which all phenomena are indestructible.

The meaning thus described is itself the absence of meaning; it is without sound, without verbal expression, without that which is signified, and without that which arises from signification. This is called knowledge, namely:
the knowledge that follows the understanding of meaning, and the knowledge that follows the understanding of consciousness.

This explanation of the meaning of *jñāna* (knowledge) is precisely the meaning of the knowledge of suchness (*tathatā*), and the meaning of the knowledge that follows after consciousness. Such ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); the meaning of that *dharmatā* is the knowledge that follows after the meaning, the knowledge that follows after consciousness, and the knowledge that follows after ultimate reality.

As the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is, so is their meaning; if it is the nature of phenomena, it is the stability of phenomena and the quiescence of phenomena. That quiescence of phenomena does not undergo any transformation. If phenomena do not transform, then the letter and the meaning are entirely equal. If the letter and the meaning are equal, this is the equality of the non-dual meaning. If that meaning is equal, the cognition of that meaning is also equal. This is precisely what is called the wisdom of equality that enters the gate of non-duality.

Thus, the conventional and the ultimate are entirely equal. Because the meaning of the conventional is equal, the equality of the meaning of emptiness is equal; because the meaning of emptiness is equal, the equality of the person (*pudgala*) is equal; because the person is equal, the equality of phenomena (*dharma*) is equal; because phenomena are equal, the equality of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) is equal; and because one awakens to that equality of resolute belief, it is itself bodhi.

“Mañjuśrī! If one has attachment or obstruction regarding the equality of form, one has obstruction regarding the eye, because the wisdom of the intrinsic nature of both form and the eye is unobstructed;

if one has attachment or obstruction regarding various views, one has obstruction regarding the body, because the wisdom of the emptiness of intrinsic nature within the bodies of those various views is unobstructed.”

If one has attachment and obstruction regarding non-firm attention (*amanasikāra*), one will have obstruction regarding the light of the Dharma, because the wisdom that investigates the self-nature of all phenomena as empty through firm attention (*manasikāra*) is unobstructed;

if one has attachment and obstruction regarding the defilement of doubt, one will have obstruction regarding liberation, because the wisdom that realizes liberation as it truly is through faith and understanding is unobstructed;

if one has attachment and obstruction regarding the defilement of laziness, one will have obstruction regarding the firm diligence of direct realization, because the nature of awakening to the teachings as they were taught is unobstructed.

If one has attachment or obstruction regarding the various hindrances, one will likewise have obstruction regarding the factors of the seven limbs of enlightenment; for the wisdom of unobstructed liberation is itself without any obstruction.
One should know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, yet they proceed through the conjunction of causes and conditions.

Bodhisattvas should skillfully understand the causes of defilement and the causes of purification within all phenomena. Once both the causes of defilement and the causes of purification have been purified, there is no longer any basis for abiding. That is to say: the arising of "mine" and the arising of views are the causes of defilement; entering into the patience regarding the dharma of non-self is the cause of purification.
The view of self and what belongs to self are the causes of defilement; inner tranquility and the absence of outward activity are the causes of purification.

Sensual desire, ill will, and harmful thoughts are causes of defilement; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, the practice of investigation, and patience are causes of purification.
The four perversions are causes of defilement; the four foundations of mindfulness are causes of purification.
The five hindrances are causes of defilement; the five faculties are causes of purification.
The six sense bases are the cause of defilement; the six recollections are the cause of purification.
The seven unwholesome factors are the cause of defilement; the seven factors of enlightenment are the cause of purification.
The eightfold wrong path is the cause of defilement; the eightfold noble path is the cause of purification.
The nine bases of resentment are causes of defilement; the nine successive meditative attainments are causes of purification.
The ten unwholesome courses of action are causes of defilement; the ten wholesome courses of action are causes of purification.
In brief, all unwholesome mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are causes of defilement;
all wholesome mental engagements are causes of purification.

Whether they be causes of defilement or causes of purification, all those phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). They are without a sentient being, without a life-span, without a nourisher, without a person (*pudgala*), without a master, without appropriation, and without agency. Like an illusion, they are signless (*animitta*), and the internal mind is tranquil.

If there is inner tranquility, that is universal quiescence; if there is universal quiescence, that is intrinsic nature; if there is the intrinsic nature of phenomena, that is non-apprehension; if there is non-apprehension, that is non-reliance; if there is non-reliance, that is like space.
One should know that all those phenomena of affliction and purification are equal to space; yet that space does not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Why is this? O Mañjuśrī!
"In this, there is not even the slightest dharma to be found that either arises or ceases.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If that is so, what is meant by the Tathāgata’s attainment of bodhi? The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"The Tathāgata has attained bodhi because he is without root and without abiding.
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is called 'root'?"
“Furthermore, what is called ‘abiding’? The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!”
Existence with a body is the root, abiding based on false discrimination.

Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess the equality of bodhi, they possess the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena; therefore, it is said that they are without root and without abode. It is because of this that the Tathāgatas manifest perfect enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī! You should know that all phenomena are quiescent and profoundly tranquil.
What is meant by "quiescence"?
What is meant by "near-peace" (*upaśama*)?
Internally it is called "tranquility," and externally it is called "near-peace. Why is this so?
Because the eye is empty, its self-nature as "I" and "mine" is also empty; this is called tranquility (*śānta*).
Having realized the emptiness of the eye, one does not grasp at forms; this is called proximate tranquility (*upaśānta*).
Because the ear is empty, the intrinsic nature of "I" and "mine" is also empty; this is called tranquility.
Having realized the emptiness of the ear, one does not apprehend sounds; this is called proximate tranquility.
Because the nose is empty, the self-nature of "I" and "mine" is also empty; this is called tranquility.
Having realized the emptiness of the nose, there is nothing to be grasped in fragrance; this is called proximate tranquility.
Because the tongue is empty, the self-nature of "I" and "mine" is also empty; this is called tranquility (*śānti*).
Having realized the emptiness of the tongue, one does not grasp at tastes; this is called proximate tranquility (*upaśama*).
Because the body is empty, its self-nature as "I" and "mine" is also empty; this is called tranquility (*śānti*).
Having realized the emptiness of the body, one touches upon that which is without grasping; this is called proximate tranquility (*upaśama*).
Because the mind is empty, the self and what belongs to the self are also empty by nature; this is called "quiescence.
Having realized the emptiness of the mind, one does not grasp at phenomena; this is called "near-quiescence."
“Mañjuśrī! The intrinsic nature of bodhi is luminous; the intrinsic nature of the mind is luminous.
For what reason is it said that their intrinsic nature is luminous?”
This means that because its very nature is undefiled, it is equal to space; its spatial nature is all-pervasive, for like the nature of space, its ultimate nature is fundamentally luminous.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, awakening has neither entry nor exit.
What is meant by 'neither entry nor exit'? "
It is called "non-entry" because there is no grasping;
it is called "non-emergence" because there is no discarding.

The Tathāgata has realized and understood this non-entry and non-emergence; that which he has realized and understood is identical to True Suchness (tathatā), being without "this" or "that," for all phenomena are free from such distinctions. Therefore, the Tathāgata manifests perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is without marks (animitta) and without an object of focus (anālambana).
What is meant by 'without marks' and 'without an object of focus'? "
That is to say, when visual consciousness is unapprehendable, this is called signlessness;
when visible forms are not perceived, this is called the absence of an object.
When auditory consciousness is unapprehendable, this is called signlessness;
When there is no sound heard, this is called the absence of an object of perception.
When olfactory consciousness finds nothing to apprehend, this is called signlessness;
when there is no fragrance smelled, this is called the absence of an object of perception.
That the tongue-consciousness has nothing to be apprehended is called signlessness;
that flavors have nothing to be tasted is called objectlessness.
That the body-consciousness has nothing to be apprehended is called signlessness.
When contact has nothing to be perceived, this is called "objectless.
When mental consciousness has nothing to be apprehended, this is called "signless";
when phenomena have no discrimination, this is called "objectless."
Mañjuśrī! All of these are the spheres of the noble ones; the entire triple world is not the sphere of the noble ones. Therefore, one should practice within the sphere of the noble ones.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is neither past, future, nor present, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time and because the three spheres are severed. As for the three spheres:
this means that the past mind does not revolve, the future consciousness has no grasping, and the present mentation is without movement."

Should that mind, intellect, and consciousness have any dwelling place, it is without discrimination yet not apart from discrimination; without conceptualization yet not apart from conceptualization; it has no past that has already been done, no future to be experienced, and no present proliferation.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Awakening is not attained by means of a body, because it has no objective referent.

That which is not attained by means of a body means that there is nothing to be cognized by visual consciousness, nor anything to be cognized by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness; because it is not something to be cognized by mind, thought, or consciousness, it is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
This explains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), namely: non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing—the purity of the three wheels.
Just as it is with the unconditioned, so should one understand conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Since phenomena lack intrinsic nature, there is no duality among phenomena.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is a term for non-differentiation.
What is meant by 'non-differentiation'? "
Furthermore, what are the names and phrases?
They are as follows: non-conceptualization is non-differentiation;
suchness is the phrase.
Non-abiding is non-differentiation;
the dharma-realm is the phrase.
The absence of manifold natures is non-differentiation.
The reality-limit is a phrase;
being without an object of focus is non-differentiation;
being immovable is a phrase.
Emptiness is non-differentiation;
signlessness is the phrase.
The absence of applied and sustained thought is non-differentiation.
Non-conceptualization is a phrase.
The absence of seeking or aspiration is non-differentiation;
the absence of sentient beings is a phrase.
The lack of self-nature in sentient beings is non-differentiation;
space is the phrase.
Non-apprehension is non-differentiation.
Non-arising is a phrase;
non-cessation is non-differentiation;
the unconditioned is a phrase.
Non-activity is non-differentiation;
awakening is the phrase.
Quiescence is non-differentiation;
Nirvana is a term;
being without grasping is non-differentiation;
non-arising is a term.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Awakening is not something that can be realized by means of the body. Why is this?
Although the body undergoes birth, it is without thought or movement, like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles; its mind is like an illusion, empty, unreal, and devoid of any volitional activity.
Mañjuśrī! If one awakens to the body and mind as they truly are, that is itself bodhi.
That which is practiced in the conventional sense is not the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), there is neither body nor mind; there is neither dharma nor non-dharma; there is neither reality nor unreality; there is neither truth nor falsehood; and there is neither speech nor non-speech.
All phenomena are bodhi. Why is this so?

Bodhi has no location and cannot be expressed by language, because it is like space, which has no location; furthermore, it is without fabrication, without arising, and without cessation, and thus cannot be expressed by language.

Because enlightenment has no location, no fabrication, no arising or ceasing, and no means of expression, when the Tathāgata examines all phenomena as they truly are and according to reality, all those phenomena are entirely beyond verbal description.
Awakening is likewise thus; when examined according to reality, it is also beyond verbal expression.
Why is this? Because language lacks substantiality and because there is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is without grasping and without containment.
What is meant by 'without grasping'? "
What is meant by "being without internal storage"?
Because one thoroughly understands the eye, it is called "having nothing to grasp";
because form is non-apprehendable, it is called "being without internal storage."
To fully understand the ear is called "having nothing to grasp";
that sound is unattainable is called "having no storehouse.
To fully understand the nose is called "having nothing to grasp";
The non-apprehension of fragrance is called "absence of containment";
the thorough knowledge of the tongue is called "absence of grasping";
the non-apprehension of taste is called "absence of containment."
Because one thoroughly understands the body, it is called "without anything to be grasped";
because contact is non-apprehendable, it is called "without internal storage.
Because one thoroughly understands the mind, it is called "without anything to be grasped."
The non-apprehension of dharmas is called being without a storehouse.
Because the Tathāgata has thus nothing to grasp and no storehouse, he has realized awakening through direct manifestation.
Having realized awakening, he grasps nothing at the eye, apprehends nothing of form, and abides in nothing within eye-consciousness.
The ear has nothing to grasp, sounds have nothing to be obtained, and ear-consciousness has no abiding;
the nose has nothing to grasp, odors have nothing to be obtained, and nose-consciousness has no abiding;
the tongue has nothing to grasp, tastes have nothing to be obtained, and tongue-consciousness has no abiding.
The body has nothing to grasp, contact is unobtainable, and body-consciousness has no abiding;
the mind has nothing to grasp, mental objects are unobtainable, and mind-consciousness has no abiding.
Because consciousness has no abiding, one is named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
You should know that there are four kinds of dharmas by which sentient beings abide in their minds. What are these four?
It refers to form, sensation, perception, and formations; all sentient beings dwell their minds within these.

Because sentient beings have a dwelling-place for their minds within these four dharmas, the Tathāgata speaks of non-arising, non-ceasing, and the absence of anything to be cognized, establishing the name "Bodhi" as emptiness.
Because awakening is empty, all phenomena are empty, and the Tathāgata is also empty; it is by means of this emptiness that he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment. Mañjuśrī!
It is not for the sake of emptiness that one realizes awakening as empty; rather, one should know that within all phenomena there is a single principle of wisdom, namely emptiness.
Because awakening is not empty, awakening is non-dual; therefore, both awakening and emptiness are without any categories.

Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally non-dual; they have no characteristics and no categories, no names and no marks, and are beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness. They are without arising and without ceasing, without activity and without non-activity, and furthermore, they are without accumulation, without letters, and without forgetfulness. It is because of this that one speaks of all phenomena as empty and without anything to be grasped. What is spoken of here is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); rather, it is said to be "empty" because within the ultimate truth, no phenomenon can be apprehended.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as space is such, that which is called ‘space’ is so named because it is ineffable. Mañjuśrī!”
Emptiness is likewise so. This emptiness that is spoken of is called "emptiness" because it is beyond words.
If one understands and enters into it in this way, then all phenomena are nameless; because they are nameless, all those phenomena are merely established through conventional designations.

Mañjuśrī! A name does not abide in any direction, nor is it separate from any direction. Just as a name does not abide in any direction and is not separate from any direction, so too are the names and designations used for phenomena spoken of; and those phenomena thus spoken of do not abide in any direction, nor are they separate from any direction. All phenomena are likewise so.

The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that from the very beginning it is thus: unborn and unceasing, without arising and without marks, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness, without words, and without sounds; as he has known it, so too is his liberation.
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that all phenomena are neither bound nor liberated. Thus ends the third fascicle of the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra:
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on Entering the Realm of All Buddhas, Adorned with the Radiance of Wisdom*.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas,
Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master, Court Scattered Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Propagator of the Sanskrit Language.
The Great Master, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Weijing, and others, translated by imperial decree.
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī!

Bodhi is equal to space; that is to say, just as space has neither height nor depth, so too bodhi has neither height nor depth. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment."
Although one has attained perfect enlightenment, there is not even a minute particle of any phenomenon—whether high or low—that is performed; to know this Dharma as it truly is is itself true wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! For what reason is it called "ultimate wisdom"?

It means that all phenomena are understood to be without root, neither arising nor ceasing; they have no real nature and are non-apprehendable. If there were a real nature, it would be a phenomenon subject to extinction. Although they arise, they lack a sovereign and are without grasping.

Mañjuśrī! If there is no master and no grasping, then dharmas are of the nature of cessation. Whether these various dharmas arise or cease, one should know that they all proceed by way of conditions; yet, within this, not even the slightest dharma can be made to proceed. Nevertheless, the Buddha-Tathāgata does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Awakening (bodhi) is the term 'just as it is spoken' (yathā-vāda).
For what reason is it called the term 'just as it is spoken'? "
As it is said, the phrase itself is bodhi.
Just as bodhi is, so too are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they do not depart from suchness.

Just as bodhi is, so too are the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the sense bases of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; they do not depart from suchness.

Just as with bodhi, so it is with the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, the odor-element, and the nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, the taste-element, and the tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, the tangible-object-element, and the body-consciousness-element; and likewise the mind-element, the mental-phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—all these do not depart from suchness.
Just as with bodhi, so it is with the earth-element, the water-element, the fire-element, and the wind-element—all these likewise do not depart from suchness.

These phenomena are thus designated; that which is designated refers to the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. It is by means of these that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment—an enlightenment that is free from all inverted dharmas.

As it is with the prior dharma, so it is with the subsequent dharma, and so it is with the intermediate dharma; the prior limit is unborn, the subsequent limit does not go away, and the intermediate limit is by nature detached. This suchness of dharmas is precisely what is called the "phrase as it has been taught."
As it is with one dharma, so it is with many dharmas;
as it is with many dharmas, so it is with one dharma. Mañjuśrī!
Whether as a single nature or as manifold natures, neither can be apprehended; whether with marks or without marks, there is neither entry nor abiding.
What is called "marks"?
What is called "without marks"?
What is called "characteristic" refers to the very arising of all wholesome dharmas;
what is called "signlessness" refers to the fact that all dharmas are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, "characteristic" refers to the state in which the mind has no place of abiding.
The signless (*animitta*) is the liberation gateway of the signless samādhi.
Furthermore, "sign" refers to the conceptualization, weighing, calculation, and investigation of all phenomena;
"signless" refers to that which transcends such weighing.
What is meant by "transcending measurement"?
It refers to the fact that consciousness does not perceive phenomena as having intrinsic existence. Furthermore, "characteristic" refers to the investigation of conditioned phenomena.
That which is signless is the investigation of the unconditioned. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
awakening is that which is untainted and without grasping.
What is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava)?
What is called "without grasping" (anupādāna)?
That which is outflow-free refers to being free from the four kinds of dharmas associated with outflows (sāsrava).
What are the four? First, the outflow of desire; second, the outflow of existence; third, the outflow of ignorance; and fourth, the outflow of views.
"Without grasping" refers to being free from these four kinds of clinging.
What are the four? First, the grasping for sensual desires; second, the grasping for views; third, the grasping for precepts and observances; and fourth, the grasping for the doctrine of self.
These four graspings all arise from being obscured by the darkness of ignorance and moistened by the dharma of craving, whereby they mutually adhere to one another.

Mañjuśrī! If one can understand that from the very beginning, grasping at the root of my words is itself my purity; once I am pure, one accordingly knows that all sentient beings are pure. Because I am pure, all those sentient beings are pure. If all sentient beings are pure, then phenomena are non-dual and of a non-dual nature; that meaning of non-duality is neither arising nor ceasing.

Mañjuśrī! If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then there is no mind, thought, or consciousness to be transformed; if there is no mind, thought, or consciousness to be transformed, then there is no conceptual differentiation;
if there is no conceptual differentiation, then ignorance does not correspond with deep and firm mental attention.
It is able to give rise [to them]; if that ignorance does not arise, then the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) will not grow;
if the twelve links of existence do not grow, then phenomena are without arising; if phenomena are without arising, then phenomena are determined;
if phenomena are determined, that is the meaning of subduing (*vinaya*); and that which is the meaning of subduing is precisely...
The ultimate truth: if it is the ultimate truth, it is the meaning of being devoid of a person (pudgala);
if it is the meaning of being devoid of a person, it is the meaning of being ineffable; if it is the meaning of being ineffable, it is the meaning of dependent origination;
if it is the meaning of dependent origination, it is the meaning of phenomena (dharma); and if it is the meaning of phenomena, it is the meaning of the Tathāgata.

As it has been said: if one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma; if one sees the Dharma, one sees the Tathāgata. Yet when those various things seen are examined with thorough and reasoned investigation, not even the slightest phenomenon is to be found therein.
Mañjuśrī! What is called "a small dharma"? It refers to that which is the object of the mind's apprehension.
If there is no mental object, then there is nothing seen; it is by virtue of such a dharma that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, for he is equal because of equality.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
Bodhi means the sense of purity, the sense of being stainless, and the sense of non-attachment.
What is meant by purity?
What is meant by being stainless?
What is called "non-attachment"?
It means that the gate of liberation of emptiness is itself purity;
the gate of liberation of signlessness is itself stainlessness.
The gate of liberation through wishlessness is itself non-attachment;
non-arising is purity; and the absence of mental formation is stainlessness.
Non-arising is non-attachment;
its intrinsic nature is purity;
perfect purity is stainlessness.
Brilliance is non-attachment;
the absence of conceptual proliferation is purity;
freedom from conceptual proliferation is stainlessness.
The cessation of conceptual proliferation is non-attachment; suchness is purity;
the dharma-realm is stainless.
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is non-attachment; space is purity;
the vast expanse is stainlessness.
Vastness is non-attachment;
thoroughly understanding internal phenomena is purity;
having no outward activity is stainlessness.
Non-apprehension of both the internal and external is non-attachment;
thorough knowledge of the phenomena of the aggregates is purity;
the intrinsic nature of the phenomena of the elements is stainlessness.
Detachment from all sense bases is non-attachment;
the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the past is purity;
the knowledge of non-arising regarding the future is stainlessness.
The wisdom that abides in the present dharmadhātu is non-attachment. Mañjuśrī!
All such meanings as these—purity, stainlessness, and non-attachment—are universally subsumed within a single phrase, namely, the phrase "quiescence."

If it is tranquil, it is thoroughly tranquil; if it is thoroughly tranquil, it is closely tranquil; if it is closely tranquil, it is stilled; and that which is stilled is said to be the Dharma of the Great Muni.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! As is space, so too is bodhi; as is bodhi, so too are all dharmas."
As are all phenomena, so too are sentient beings;
as are sentient beings, so too are the buddha-fields;
as are the buddha-fields, so too is nirvāṇa.

Mañjuśrī! This teaching is the equality of nirvāṇa; it is the cause for the ultimate limit and purity of all phenomena. It is without antidote and free from the cause of antidotes; it is primordially pure, primordially stainless, and primordially unattached.

Because the Tathāgata has realized that all phenomena possess such characteristics, he manifests perfect enlightenment; thereafter, observing the realms of sentient beings, he establishes the dharma-gate of pure, stainless, and unattached play, and through these names, his great compassion toward all sentient beings is set in motion.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is the conduct of a bodhisattva? What is the supreme practice of a bodhisattva?"
That is to say, if a bodhisattva is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible, neither born nor unborn, they do not apprehend any mark of ultimate exhaustion, yet they do not destroy ultimate non-arising.
“Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva practices in this way, this is the supreme practice of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!”
The Bodhisattva’s past mind has already ceased; herein there is no activity.
The future mind has not yet arrived; herein there is no activity.
The present mind does not abide; herein there is no activity.
The Bodhisattva is entirely without attachment toward all minds of the past, future, and present; if a Bodhisattva practices in this manner, this is the supreme practice of a Bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, regarding the dharma of giving, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas are non-dual and of one kind; if a Bodhisattva practices in this way, it is the supreme practice of a Bodhisattva."

It is likewise with morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas are non-dual and of one kind. If a Bodhisattva practices in this manner, this constitutes the supreme practice of a Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva does not practice the emptiness of form, nor does he practice the non-emptiness of form. If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, this is called the supreme practice of a bodhisattva."
Why is this? Form is itself emptiness;

the intrinsic nature of form is empty. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Therefore, one does not practice the emptiness of consciousness, nor does one practice the non-emptiness of consciousness. If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, this constitutes the supreme practice of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? It is because mind, thought, and consciousness are non-apprehendable. Mañjuśrī!
Within this, there is not even the slightest dharma that can exist—whether it be known or abandoned, cultivated or realized—all of these are utterly non-existent.
Because it is thus, this is called "exhaustion" (kṣaya).
This is what constitutes the characteristic of ultimate exhaustion; if there is ultimate exhaustion, there is nothing to be exhausted, and even this "non-exhaustion" is itself non-existent.
Why? Because it is exhausted in accordance with what has been taught.

If, as it has been said, there is exhaustion, then there is no dharma that can be exhausted. If there is no dharma that can be exhausted, this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). That which is unconditioned neither arises nor ceases. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains eternally present. Because the Dharma abides, it is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Because it abides like the realm of phenomena, wisdom neither undergoes transformation nor is it without transformation. Since wisdom neither transforms nor is without transformation, one who awakens to and enters into such a principle of the Dharma attains the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the non-arising, and the non-ceasing; this is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Mañjuśrī! Therefore, you should know that although there is the conventional designation of a collection of sounds and letters, therein not even the slightest dharma arises or ceases.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha. He offered praise with these sublime verses:
“Formless and without manifest color, devoid of characteristics, Within it there is neither cessation nor arising;
Neither abiding nor even a fundamental basis exists— To the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now offer praise and prostration.”
Because of non-abiding, there is neither entering nor exiting, nor are there any such stages;
having already attained liberation from the gateway of the six sense bases, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referents.
Abiding nowhere among all phenomena, Transcending both existence and non-existence,
Perfectly accomplishing the equality of all conditioned things— To the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage and praise.
Having already attained liberation from the three realms, you abide in the state of equality like space;
with a mind untainted by worldly desires, I now praise and prostrate to the Venerable One who is free from all objective referents.
Always abiding in meditative equipoise, even while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;
with all postures perfectly composed and solemn—I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
Coming with equanimity and departing with equanimity, Abiding wondrously within the state of equanimity,
The Dharma-gate of the indestructible nature of equanimity— To the Venerable One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage.
The Great Sage has skillfully entered into the nature of equality; all phenomena abide within his mind of meditative equipoise.
Having universally entered the wondrous dharma-gate of signlessness, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
The Great Sage abides nowhere and has no object of focus; Within meditative concentration, he has loftily accumulated the peaks of wisdom.
He has attained perfect realization throughout all phenomena; To the Honored One who has no object of focus, I now pay homage and praise.
The majestic deportment and physical forms of sentient beings, as well as their speech and voices—these he can manifest everywhere in a single instant;
I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
The Great Sage has already transcended name and form, And has universally severed the aggregates, elements, and phenomena;
Furthermore, he is able to skillfully enter the gate of signlessness— To the Honored One who is without objective referent, I now pay homage and praise.
The Great Sage has skillfully transcended all marks, And is likewise far removed from the realm of marks;
Having successfully entered the gate of signlessness, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referents.
Without thought or conceptualization, with a pure mind that likewise abides nowhere;
free from all mental engagements and the arising of recollection—to the One without an object of focus, I now pay homage and praise.
Just as space contains nothing within it, Having transcended conceptual proliferation and is free from attachment, Your mind is equanimous like the sky;
To you, the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage.
Just as space has neither center nor periphery, so too is the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas;
having already transcended the gateway of the three times, I now praise and pay homage to the One who is without objective referent.
The Buddhas are like the nature of space, and this very space is itself without marks;
having attained liberation from both phenomena and their causes, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is free from all objects of perception.
Among all phenomena there is no dependence; like the moon in water, there is nothing to grasp.
Without the mark of self and without sound, you who have no object of perception—O Honored One, I now praise and pay homage to you.
The Great Sage does not rely upon the dharmas of the aggregates; the same is true for the dharmas of the elements and sense-bases.
Having already liberated the mind from inverted views, I now praise and pay homage to the Venerable One who is without any objective referent.
The Great Sage has already transcended the two extremes, And has likewise severed the view of a self;
Having attained the perfect realization of the equality of the dharma-realm, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
Already liberated from the names and numbers of forms and signs, And likewise far removed from all unrighteous dharmas,
With a mind of equality that neither grasps nor rejects, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of perception.
Having already transcended all magical arts, you have attained complete mastery over all phenomena;
you have wondrously entered the dharma-gate of non-obstruction—O Venerable One who has no objective referent, I now pay homage to you in praise.
With right wisdom, you do not say that phenomena exist, nor do you say that phenomena do not exist;
you are beyond the path of speech and without arising—to you, the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage.
The Sage does not rely upon dualistic dharmas; long ago he shattered the banner of self-conceit.
He has attained liberation through the gateway of non-duality and the two truths—to that Honored One who is without objective referent, I now pay homage and praise.
All faults of body, speech, and mind have long since been universally severed by the Great Sage;
beyond analogy and inconceivable, I now praise and prostrate to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
The Great Sage has no turning back and no awakening; he is utterly free from all faults.
With wisdom as his forerunner, he pervades all conduct. To the Honored One who is without objective referent, I now offer praise and prostration.
Untainted, pure mindfulness is most subtle and wondrous; you fully understand all phenomena, both real and unreal.
Being free from attachment and devoid of conceptual thought, O Honored One who has no objective referent, I now pay homage to you in praise.
The Great Sage has no object of focus within his mind, yet he is able to know all minds;
nor does there arise in him any conception of self or other—to you, the Honored One who has no object of focus, I now offer praise and prostration.
Within the objectless there is an object; you are not deluded or attached to any mind.
Having attained the perfect clarity of the unobstructed Dharma, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of perception.
The Great Sage has no object of focus within the mind, And likewise, his intrinsic nature is non-existent.
Through a mindless equanimity, he has attained perfect realization; I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of focus.
The Great Sage does not rely on the dharma of wisdom, yet is able to universally observe all buddha-fields;
likewise, he perceives the conduct of all sentient beings—homage now to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
The wise find nothing to be grasped within the mind, And therein it is likewise ultimately non-existent;
To the Honored One who possesses perfect and universal knowledge of all phenomena, Who is without any object of perception—to you I now pay homage.
Knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, And that these very illusions are likewise non-existent,
Having attained liberation through this gateway of illusory phenomena— To you, the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage and praise.
Although the Perfectly Awakened One moves within the world, he does not rely upon worldly phenomena;
furthermore, he is free from worldly conceptualization. To the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now pay homage.
The Great Sage traverses that very space; through space, he has realized the realm of emptiness.
That which is empty and non-empty is what the Sage proclaims; I now pay homage to the Venerable One who is without objective referent.
Manifesting great supernormal powers and performing transformative deeds, All relying upon the illusion-like samādhi,
Entering the universal gateway that is free from manifold natures— I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is without objective referent.
Thoroughly knowing the nature of neither oneness nor multiplicity, neither shifting toward the near nor the far,
with a mind of equality that is neither high nor low— to the Honored One who has no object of perception, I now offer praise and prostration.
The diamond-like concentration manifests before him; in a single instant, he attains perfect enlightenment.
He has universally entered the dharma-gate of non-obstruction; I now praise and pay homage to the Venerable One who is without an object of perception.
Though you know nirvāṇa to be unmoving, you have also skillfully disciplined yourself throughout the three times;
endowed with all manner of gateways of expedient means, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who is free from all objective referents.
Regarding all classes of sentient beings, you possess excellent understanding of wisdom and skillful means, yet you remain unmoved from the gate of nirvāṇa;
I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of perception.
The Great Sage is signless and free from awakening; having transcended conceptual proliferation, he is without obstruction.
Because he is without self, his mind is unobstructed; I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of perception.
Having already abandoned doubt and being free from fault, Likewise devoid of self and what belongs to self,
Possessing perfect and universal knowledge regarding all things, I now praise and pay homage to the Honored One who has no object of perception.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas,
Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Court Scattered Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Zhu Fonian:
I prostrate to the One who crosses the afflictions by means of the ten powers; I prostrate to the One who extensively bestows fearlessness;
To the One who dwells well within the unique dharmas; I prostrate to the World-Honored One, the Most Victorious.
I prostrate to the one who can sever all fetters; I prostrate to the one who has already reached the further shore;
I prostrate to the Honored One who rescues the world from all sufferings; I prostrate to the one who does not abide in birth and death.
Universally penetrating the conduct of sentient beings, Free from mental constructs in all places,
Like a lotus unsoiled by water, They constantly dwell in pure emptiness and silent stillness.
The various unsurpassed phrases of the Holy Teacher— I bow my head to the one who, without conditions, crosses the sea of defilement,
Who universally and skillfully contemplates all gateways of characteristics, And for whom there is nothing to be sought among all desires.
The Buddha’s great power is inconceivable, like space, without dependence;
I prostrate to the one who upholds the gateway of vast and supreme virtues; I prostrate to the one who is as sublime as Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī!”

"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī, do not give rise to the perception of form regarding the Buddhas; do not say that all phenomena are signless; do not say that the Buddhas dwell alone in the dharma-realm, nor say that the Buddha dwells amidst a great assembly. You should know that all Buddhas are without seeing and without hearing, without anything to be offered and no one who offers; of all the Tathāgatas, there is not the slightest dharma—whether of a single nature or of manifold natures—that can be performed."

Furthermore, do not say that the Buddha has attained the fruit of enlightenment, nor say that the Buddha has any dharma to manifest; there is no seeing, no hearing, no thinking, and no knowing. The Buddha likewise has no speech—neither that which has been spoken, is being spoken, nor will be spoken regarding any dharmas.

Furthermore, it is not that the Buddhas manifestly attain perfect enlightenment, nor is there any dharma by which they can attain perfect enlightenment; nor do the Buddhas sever defilement to realize purity, for whatever they do is free from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, you should know that all phenomena are primordially pure. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

You should know that the merit of this sutra is inconceivable. Suppose there were a bodhisattva who caused all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, to universally establish themselves in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, yet failed to give rise to faith and understanding toward this true Dharma.

If there are bodhisattvas who give rise to faith and understanding toward this true Dharma, the merit they obtain will be vastly greater and immeasurably more than the preceding mass of merit; how much more so for those who write it themselves or instruct others to write it, the resulting mass of merit being many times more excellent still.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person who caused all classes of sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, neither with perception nor without perception; whether bipedal, quadrupedal, legless, or many-legged—to universally establish them all so that they attain human bodies, and having attained human bodies, causes them all to give rise to the mind of great bodhicitta."

Having generated the great bodhicitta, each and every bodhisattva, for as many *kalpas* as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, provided offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, seating, medicinal requisites for illness, and various articles of pleasure to Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and assemblies of śrāvakas—each as numerous as motes of dust—within inconceivable Buddha-fields numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges. After those respective Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, they constructed stūpas made of the seven precious gems, one *yojana* wide and one hundred *yojanas* high, adorned with the finest jewels, pearls, and exquisite ornaments; they erected various jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies, and draped them with nets of sovereign king-jewels, creating manifold adornments.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose deep mind is pure, who, having heard this profound and sublime Dharma—the illumination of wisdom for entering the realm of all Buddhas and its majestic adornments—believes and understands it, or even enters into realization, and gives rise to a pure mind to expound it for others, even if only briefly as a single four-line verse, the merit obtained thereby is beyond measure. It realizes the Buddha-wisdom in the present and accomplishes the supreme deeds of meritorious conduct. Compared to the mass of merit from the previous Bodhisattva’s giving, it exceeds it such that the former does not equal one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor one-hundred-thousandth part, nor one-ten-billionth part, nor one-hundred-thousand-ten-billionth part; it does not equal any fraction, number, count, or analogy, nor even a *upaniṣad* (a minute fraction) thereof.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a lay bodhisattva who, for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, provided and made offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick to as many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River."

Suppose there is a renunciant bodhisattva whose conduct is pure and who is endowed with a profound resolve; if, among all the gathered cattle and livestock, they were to give even a single meal as a small gift, the mass of merit obtained from this would not equal even a hundredth part of the former mass of merit, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-billionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part. It does not even bear comparison by way of calculation, enumeration, analogy, or even the *upaniṣad* (the infinitesimal). It is not even a fraction of it.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were as many renunciant bodhisattvas in a trichiliocosm as there are atoms of dust, and each of them were endowed with practice and possessed a pure, profound resolve. If each of these bodhisattvas were to provide offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick to all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas throughout the worlds of the ten directions—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges in incalculable aeons—then the mass of merit obtained by those bodhisattvas would be immeasurable."

If there is a bodhisattva, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, who is fully endowed with ethical conduct and possesses a deeply pure mind, and having heard this true Dharma, gains faith and understanding, and either writes it down themselves or instructs others to write it—then the merit obtained by this person surpasses the mass of merit from the previous bodhisattva’s giving many times over; the former does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi, nor any calculation, number, or analogy of the latter.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, were to give in charity and make offerings to Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and others, filling that trichiliocosm with the seven treasures."

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding this true Dharma, is able to understand and enter into it even as briefly as a single four-line verse, the merit obtained by this person would surpass the previous mass of merit such that the former does not equal one-hundredth part of it, nor one-thousandth part, nor one-hundred-thousand-koṭi parts; it cannot be reached by calculation, nor by analogy.
“Mañjuśrī! Let alone the meritorious conduct of giving for as many eons as there are atoms in three thousandfold world systems. Mañjuśrī!”

Suppose there were as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in incalculable *gaṅgā* rivers, and each of these bodhisattvas, within as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in incalculable *gaṅgā* rivers, were to universally provide offerings day after day to as many Buddha-Bhagavāns as there are grains of sand in incalculable *gaṅgā* rivers. They would do so by constructing exquisite jewel-trees made of Jambūnada gold, draped with wonderful garments and nets of luminous pearl-maṇi jewels; by erecting pavilions made of *vaśavarti-rāja* maṇi jewels, with boundary paths made of lightning-light maṇi jewels; and by setting up exquisite banners, streamers, and precious canopies—having thus completed these in full—and practicing such acts of giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in incalculable *gaṅgā* rivers.

If there is a bodhisattva who, having developed faith and understanding in this most supreme and profound true Dharma, explains even a single four-line verse to other bodhisattvas in accordance with the truth so that they may understand and enter it, the mass of merit obtained by this [latter] bodhisattva exceeds the mass of merit from the former bodhisattva’s gift; the latter does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi, nor any calculation, number, or analogy of the former.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose the three realms have been formed, and among all the classes of sentient beings within the destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, there is a lay bodhisattva who universally rescues and delivers all those sentient beings from the destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; having caused them to attain liberation, he establishes them all in the fruit of a pratyekabuddha."
If there is an ordained bodhisattva who, among a multitude of cattle and livestock, gives even a single meal as a small gift, the merit obtained thereby is beyond measure.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Suppose that within all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions— fields as numerous as unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of atoms—
there were renunciant bodhisattvas, and each of those bodhisattvas [were to act] throughout the worlds of the ten directions..."
In every single direction of the realms, there are Buddha-worlds as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
in each of those, there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, together with their assemblies of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas,
who have passed through a period of time equal to the number of atoms in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
For kalpas, with food and drink, clothing, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
he offered to each and every one of those Buddhas and Tathāgatas daily,
filling worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of unspeakable Buddha-fields with exquisite *vaiḍūrya* and *maṇi* jewels of sovereign kings.
Regarding the offering of precious gifts:

if a bodhisattva, having developed faith and understanding in this true Dharma, gives even a small amount from among their cattle and livestock, down to a single meal, the merit obtained thereby exceeds the mass of merit from the previous bodhisattva’s gift; the former does not approach one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even one-hundred-thousand-koṭi-fold of that merit, nor can it be expressed by any calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Because if one hears this True Dharma now, one immediately attains the Great Wisdom Seal of the non-retrogressive Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who is able to cause all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions to be established and made to dwell upon the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhānusārin*);

yet, if there is another bodhisattva who establishes a single sentient being and causes them to dwell upon the stage of practice through dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the merit obtained by the latter is beyond measure.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who can establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions and cause them to abide on the stage of practice in accordance with the meaning (arthānusāri-pratipatti-bhūmi);

and if there is another bodhisattva who establishes a single sentient being and causes them to abide on the stage of practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusāri-pratipatti-bhūmi)—the merit obtained by the latter is beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who can establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to dwell on the stage of practice in accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmapratipatti-bhūmi);
and if there is another bodhisattva who establishes a single sentient being, causing them to dwell in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala)—the merit obtained by the latter is beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there were a bodhisattva who could establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to abide in the fruit of a srotāpanna;
and if there were another bodhisattva who established a single sentient being, causing them to abide in the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin—the merit obtained by the latter would be beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there were a bodhisattva who could establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions and cause them to dwell in the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin;
and if there were another bodhisattva who established a single sentient being and caused them to dwell in the fruit of an anāgāmin—the merit obtained by the latter would be beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there were a bodhisattva who could establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to abide in the fruit of anāgāmin;
and if there were another bodhisattva who established a single sentient being, causing them to abide in the fruit of arhat—there would be no measure to the merit obtained by the latter."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there were a bodhisattva who could establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions and cause them to abide in the fruit of arhatship;
and if there were another bodhisattva who established a single sentient being and caused them to abide in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood—the merit obtained by the latter would be beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there were a bodhisattva who could establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to abide in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood;

and if there were another bodhisattva who, for the sake of a single sentient being, establishes them so that they give rise to the mind of great bodhi—the merit obtained by the latter is beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who can establish all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment;
and if there is another bodhisattva who establishes a single sentient being, causing them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression—the merit obtained by the latter is beyond measure."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Suppose a bodhisattva were to establish all sentient beings universally, causing them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression;

yet, if there were another bodhisattva who, having conceived a pure mind and given rise to faith and understanding toward this most supreme and profound True Dharma, were able to write it out himself or instruct others to do so, or even extensively proclaim it for others—to the point of enabling even a single sentient being to have faith, understanding, and realization regarding this most supreme and profound True Dharma—the mass of merit obtained would be immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond reckoning."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of the great assembly:
"If there are bodhisattvas who, throughout the full extent of time, Make offerings to ten koṭis of Buddhas And uphold this gateway of the True Dharma,"
Furthermore, if one delights in hearing and receiving the profound scriptures,
this merit is vast and boundless, the most supreme among all rewards.
If there are bodhisattvas who travel to the ten directions by means of their supernormal powers,
In the presence of ten koṭis of Buddhas, he drew near and made offerings;
he paid homage everywhere to the Honored Ones among Men, the most supreme of all holy beings,
who out of compassion for all sentient beings increase their manifold benefit and happiness.
This most profound sutra is proclaimed by all Buddhas together;
if one can expound it for others even for a moment,
this is the very opening of pure faith within the Buddha’s teaching.
The fruit of merit obtained thereby is vast and most supreme.
Out of great compassion, all Buddhas proclaim this True Dharma, which,
like the light of a vast lamp, universally illuminates the realms of humans and devas.
Among them, those with sharp and penetrating wisdom, as well as those endowed with great power, can give rise to a mind of faith and resolve, swiftly attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.
Such is the teaching of the Sugata; if there are any who hear it, [they shall likewise attain it].
Having heard it, they in turn proclaim it to others, passing it on from one to another.
Just as for those Buddhas, the most honored among men,
who have entered the great nirvāṇa without remainder and attained purity.
One is able to erect a precious stūpa, towering high and most exquisite,
adorned with various jewels, surpassing the limits of the Peak of Existence.
Upon it are raised magnificent banners and canopies, and from its jeweled bells issue forth wondrous sounds.
Reaching upward to the Peak of Existence, it is magnificent and vast.
If there are bodhisattvas who love and delight in this sutra,
and having heard it within such a manifestation, they give rise to pure faith,
In that pure place, this True Dharma is established;
the mass of merit obtained therein is vast and most supreme.
If there are bodhisattvas who uphold this True Dharma, [they shall attain great benefit].
Extensively circulating it for others, one washes away the stain of stinginess regarding the Dharma;
the mass of merit thus obtained is infinitely superior,
and as one seeks great enlightenment, it shall be attained according to one's vows.
This profound sutra, proclaimed by all Buddhas,
is upheld and expounded by the great assembly of Bodhisattvas.
All Buddhas of the ten directions, throughout the entire realm of empty space, [proclaim it as well].
“Universally manifesting the bodies of all Buddhas, causing all beings to gaze upon them in reverence.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, along with countless, inconceivable, and ineffable multitudes of other bodhisattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
